en: The Narrative of the Vow of Day and Night. Om! Homage to the Glorious Dharmadhātu!
He is pure as space, arisen, and the locus of qualities free from conceptual proliferation.
Homage to him whose nature is the stūpa, who consists of the five aggregates and is peaceful.

Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great community of monks, along with many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas;
with a multitude of elder monks who were free from passion; with hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas; and with a vast number of śrāvakas.
Surrounded by the ten world-protectors, the deities of the Four Great Kings, and many humans of the four castes, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands,
all the people in that assembly hall who were listeners of the Dharma gazed upon the Blessed One and remained seated, reflecting upon the discourse concerning the vow of the *caitya*.
Then the elder Subhūti rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, circumambulated [the Blessed One] three times, placed his right knee upon the ground,
bowed to the Blessed One, and said this: "O Protector, at what time is the one-night-and-day vow (ahorātravrata) observed?"
And tell me, O Lord of all worlds, what is the procedure for that; tell me all of it.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! You who have compassion for sentient beings, listen;
I shall explain to you the procedure for the perpetual vow of day and night."
In the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, there was a city named Gandhavatī;
in it dwelt a king of great majesty and supreme power, named Indrapṛṣṭha.

Having prepared an assembly hall within his inner apartments, he rose suddenly, prostrated before Vasubandhu, the teacher of the world, and joyfully questioned him according to the prescribed ritual. (Avk 5)
I wish to hear all of that which is the most excellent among vows,
by the power of whose merit beings attain perfect nirvāṇa.
O steadfast one, compassionate toward all beings, speak all of that;
for you must protect this world which is agitated by evil deeds.
Vasubandhu said: Listen, O King, to what I shall proclaim—the supreme among vows, the Ahorātra-vrata, which was previously expounded by Vipaśyin. (Avk 8)
On the full moon day of the month of Aśvinī, one should perform a vow of great success;
being pure, one should likewise worship the Caitya with sixteen ritual procedures.
On the thirteenth day, at the conclusion of the meal, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth and so forth;
on the fourteenth day, in particular, one should have the work of shaving performed.
Having bathed in sacred fords and being clothed in clean garments,
the wise one should worship the shrine at midday and cause a lamp to be offered.
When the sun has reached the sixth part [of its course], one should consume milk-rice;
then, having again performed purification and other rites, one should joyfully listen to the Dharma. (Avk 12)
At dawn on the full moon day, having bathed, one should commence the vow;
first, having purified the surface of the ground, one should cause a hall of Dharma to be constructed. (Avk 13)
One should bathe the preeminent Caitya with very cool perfumed waters,
and with cow's milk and the five jewels, one should smear it with stone ash.
Four banners should be set up, along with canopies and yak-tail whisks;
one should hang a garland of directions made of various flowers within the temple of the Jina.
Thereafter, having undertaken the vow, one should bow to the Guru as Vajradhara;
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, one should meditate upon the Dharmadhātu.

The shrine consisting of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is the supreme abode of the Victors; it is declared to be the beginningless Buddha, the dwelling place of all Tathāgatas, and the shrine that is the abode of all gods. Having propitiated this shrine, one should observe the vow. (Avk 17)
Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, radiant with the luster of the moon's orb, red in color, born from the syllable *bhoḥ*, and resplendent with four faces. (Avk 18)
The root face is red and white; the right face is reddish like saffron; the western face is as red as a lotus; and the northern face is yellowish-red. Avk 19.
One should visualize the Lord of Speech, the Teacher of the World, resplendent with eight arms;
holding a bow and arrow with two hands, and likewise holding a noose and a goad,
as well as a book of wisdom, a sword, and a vajra-bell with the others.
Endowed with all flavors, seated in a graceful posture, his body adorned with divine ornaments and wearing a crown of the five Buddhas. // Avk_21 //
Having thus visualized Vāgīśvara, who is great white and established in all phenomena,
within one's own heart, one should place him before oneself and worship him.
Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful oblation (argha), endowed with devotion,
[he should worship] with fragrant flowers born of water and land, and with the five fragrances.
With fragrant substances that cause union, with excellent incenses and fumigations, with lamps fed with ghee, and with food offerings consisting of divine delicacies; // Avk_24 //
With parasols, banners, and flags; with dance, song, and beautiful instrumental music;
and likewise with fruits, roots, leaves, betel nut, and betel leaf.
With various medicinal herbs, both divine and human, as well as with jasmine flowers, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, parched grain, and the five jewels; Avk_26 //
One should offer an oblation of milk, conch-shells, and fine flowers at the preeminent Caitya;
one should recite the Dhāraṇī and the hymn, and have songs sung. Avk 27.
And being filled with joy, one should perform a thousand circumambulations;
throughout the full course of day and night, one should continue to practice circumambulation. (Avk 28)
In whichever temple or sacred ford one worships all the gods,
one must never allow contact with those of low birth.
If such contact occurs, one should perform ritual bathing and purify oneself by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Even when there is no physical contact, one who observes the vow should perform ritual bathing and practice it during the three junctions of the day.
{CD adds the following after 'śodhayet':
the pure sequence, as well as the supreme Dharma, the vow of day and night.}
When there is an increase in the number of days, one should not perform it; even if capable, one should have it performed [at the correct time].

O King, one should observe a vow by indulging in sleep—that is, by taking rest—and likewise by indulging in repose; however, since there is a fault in doing so, one should not observe it in that way. A practitioner of the vow should not indulge in sleep throughout the full duration of day and night.
Endowed with meditation on the caitya, one should practice while reciting the mantra and chanting the hymn.
One should perform circumambulation with various songs and great enthusiasm, with dances, resonant musical instruments, shouts of "Hā Hā," and exultations. (Avk 32)
One whose mind is intent on the vow should neither seek rest nor feel weariness;
when the day and night are fully completed, one should bathe in the morning and perform the vow.
Having performed worship of the caityas, one should likewise perform worship of the guru,
offering food, clothing, gold, rice, jewels, and ornaments.
It should be offered to the preceptor with great devotion according to one's ability;
thereafter, the wielder of the vajra should perform the sacrifice and bring the vow to completion.
Then, having bestowed the consecration, as well as the five threads and the vase,
and having given these individually to each of those observing the vows, one should cause the benediction to be granted.
Having performed the worship of Kaumārī, one should consume the remaining food;
curd combined with sugar constitutes the excellent meal of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then, one who knows the ritual should perform the *gaṇacakra* according to its prescribed method;
thus, whoever performs this King of Vows with a pure mind— (Avk 38)
Having enjoyed vast wealth and being endowed with every happiness,
O Lord of the Earth, one attains happiness in the next world in the realm of Dharma.
Indrapṛṣṭa said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, Knower of All, you ought to speak again:
how is it that their births occur in many ways within saṃsāra?"
Tell me now all of this: the entire fruit of the vow-worship, the time, the occasion, and the day; and in what place the vow is to be performed. Avk 41.
Vasubandhu said:
Listen, O fortunate King, as I speak in brief of the most excellent merit specifically regarding this place of the Self-Existent One.
In its absence, [one should offer] in one's own country, at a stationary shrine or a preeminent sacred site;
in its absence, having performed it oneself or likewise caused it to be performed by others.
Whether made of gold, or of jewels and other minerals, likewise of stone, wood, bricks, or clay; Avk_44 //
On a cloth made from a ball of rice mixed with sand, or when it has been painted, in a temple, on a riverbank, at a sacred ford, or upon a holy spot of earth; Avk_45 //
Having first purified the Dharma-hall according to the rules, one should observe the vow;
and with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, fragrant scents, and water, [one should worship] the preeminent Caitya.
One should first offer the *argha* to the Sun and scatter flowers along with parched grain;
then, one should draw the mandala of the five deities using cow-dung and water.
One should sprinkle the practitioners with water joined by non-futile syllables;
[one should establish] the practitioner upon the head with mantras whose final syllables are *havarga*. (Avk 48)

Having performed the binding of the directions with the threatening mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, and having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should pay homage to the Guru. (Avk 49)
Holding flowers and unbroken rice grains in his hand, he should cast three handfuls of flowers [into the vessel],
which has arisen from the five elements and rests upon the pericarp of a lotus.
One should invoke the radiant Vāgīśvara, who is the Dharmadhātu;
having drawn him in as the embodiment of gnosis and established him within the pledge, one should worship him.
I invoke you, O Lord; stay there in that enchanting place.
Be ever steadfast, do not depart; grant your presence in this stationary abode.
May he accept with joy this *argha* offered by me, consisting of milk, unbroken rice, and water, together with the nine gems and gold, placed within a conch shell. Avk 53.
O Lord of Great Radiance, may you accept these divine silken garments and robes, variegated with many colors; may you rejoice.
Let sandalwood from the Malaya mountains, musk, saffron, and the like,
as well as śaileya and camphor, be taken and approved.
Taking flowers—those born of water, those born of land, and those divine—strung together with five-colored threads and imbued with the fragrance of great joy, may you rejoice! (Avk 56)
This incense, well-blended with divine fragrance, satisfies the sense of smell;
it is offered for your gratification—please accept it, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees.
This lamp, which dispels darkness and destroys all blindness, is ablaze with ghee and oil; it has been offered by me—please accept it.
O Protector, may there be happiness for me as they enjoy the four kinds of food, the six kinds of flavors, and meals consisting of ghee and sugar. Avk 59.
Take the various fruits, the beautiful blossoms, the silk-cotton trees, the kāraṇḍava ducks, and so forth; take the trunks, roots, and leaves—may you rejoice!
For the sake of your welfare, please accept these betel leaves combined with areca nuts, pure camphor, and various collections of divine medicinal herbs.
With a benevolent mind, please accept these parched grains, unbroken rice, fruits, and *dūrvā* and *kunda* flowers, which have been offered by me to you with devotion. (Avk 62)
Holding up parasols made of gold and other materials, various banners,
and all manner of flags and streamers, may the Jina rejoice!
The wise one, having performed worship in that manner, should likewise offer praise;
for the sake of pleasing the Lord of Jinas, he should also perform circumambulations. (Avk 64)
I pay homage to the reliquary of the Jina, which consists of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), which manifests in the form of all worlds,
and which is the abode of all Buddhas.
Homage to you, who manifest the relics of the Victors with playful ease;
I constantly take refuge in you, the bliss of the commitment of the three vehicles.

I bow to that which is born of the Victor, which abides in all things, the field of merit, which bestows the desired objects upon those who serve it for the sake of the happiness of holy beings. (Avk 67)
I bow to the best of sages, the bestower of the purpose of auspiciousness, the destroyer of the fears of people, the Lord of the World, Maheśvara. Avk_68 //
The deities residing in all worlds have assembled in the maṇḍala of the Victor;
therefore, one should offer them a bali-offering with devotion and worship for their satisfaction.
{CD After verse 69, add the following:

Having performed the purification, beautification, and other rites, one should adorn the practitioner with golden earrings, all ornaments, garments such as those from the Ganges, and garlands of flowers.}
One should kindle a circular hearth of iron and extensively offer fragrant incense before it; this pacifies all misdeeds.
One should also [offer] many auspicious musical instruments, parasols, and vessels of vermilion.
And the teacher should cause a great festival to be celebrated with words of auspicious blessing.
On the full moon day of Aśvinī, on a Sunday,
and specifically when joined with the Āyuṣmatī yoga, it is especially auspicious.
O Lord of the Earth, whoever performs a vow during that [time] shall obtain abundant enjoyment;
having attained happiness in the next world, they will dwell in the realm of the Jina.
Listen, O highly fortunate King; I shall speak again of the fruit of worship,
by which one who has established a caitya becomes free from sorrow,
liberated from illusion and delusion, and untainted by the three impurities.
Those who bathe the image of a Jina’s shrine with the five nectars and the essence of sandalwood fragrance,
they bring forth delight with the Apsarases through the sweet scents of the waters of the Mandākinī.
Those people who offer incense here for even a moment never experience sorrow;
their lotus-feet are worshipped by gods and asuras, and their bodies are adorned with fragrant garlands and garments.
People with serene minds constantly offer fragrances to him;
those worlds become worlds of ultimate reality, their bodies fragrant and radiant as the sun and moon.

Those who offer fine garments adorned with saffron and other pigments to the Tathāgatas at the caityas shall never experience the suffering of cold; by that cause, their treasury shall become vast and substantial.
To you, who possess all flowers born of water— white, reddish, dark, bright yellow, and black—
and who belong to a noble lineage for the sake of Samantabhadra, health and happiness arise from your giving.
Those people who, devoted to faith, perform worship with noble, fragrant garlands and many flowers out of great devotion, obtain all forms of happiness in the world.

Those who arrange rows of lamps for the Buddha— [lamps] pleasing to the eye, containing many precious jewels, whose lotus-feet are honored by kings, and which, like the lamp of wisdom, destroy the web of delusion— Avk_80.

In this world, he who, endowed with devotion, offers to him an oblation that is delicious and fragrant, becomes powerful and distinguished, his feet worshipped by the crest-jewels of the circle of kings and served by monarchs. (Avk 81)
Having offered fruits, roots, and other such things at the shrines with a devoted mind, one obtains the desired fruit, remaining free from disease and always happy. (Avk 82)

Those who are liberated from diseases and other powerful causes of suffering, possessing gentle countenances and a lovely complexion like gold, obtain a kingdom free from thorns; this they desire by means of the practice of giving medicine at a shrine.
Having offered the group of items beginning with betel, one who is handsome, happy,
and pure shall obtain a divine woman who captivates the mind and the fortune of royalty.

The fortunate one, worthy of worship throughout the three worlds, possessing a vast lineage and protected by his virtues, has been born with a body of intensely radiant splendor; he spreads a high canopy over the stupa.
Those who, endowed with devotion, offer banners and flags at a shrine or an image,
become lords of the earth who have conquered the hosts of the wicked, and they become protectors both in heaven and on earth.
With joyful hearts, they provide and offer parasols adorned with various precious jewels;
honored by hosts of lords of the earth, they become endowed with glory and devoted to the Dharma at the shrines.

Those who offer resonant sounds at a shrine with lutes and other instruments, with bells, mṛdaṅga drums, and horns, and with the divine sounds of conchs and the like, shall rely upon the five superknowledges.
One should constantly cause dance to be performed before the Jina with songs that inspire great enthusiasm and possess most charming melodies, and one should also make divine proclamations.
Those people become melodious-voiced and handsome, both in heaven and on earth;
possessing divine hearing and great wisdom, they shall always hear beautiful sounds.
Having performed dance, song, and other such acts before a shrine, an image, or a temple of the Jina,
those of noble lineage are honored, become free from sin, and possess great learning.
Those who perform auspicious deeds become long-lived, endowed with a thousand eyes, free from calamities, and the locus of virtues; their limbs are liberated from planetary influences and diseases.
Those who stand with weapons in hand in the abode of the Jina, endowed with devotion to the Jina, are for the purpose of terrifying wicked beings and for the sake of protection. // Avk_93 //
Long-lived, free from disease, endowed with sons and grandsons,
fortunate and wealthy in riches, they go at the end to the abode of the Jina.
With devotion, one should cast *dūrvā* grass, *kunda* flowers, unbroken rice grains,
and parched grain into the shrines of the Jinas while reciting words of auspiciousness.
The one who delights the world is never born into an evil destiny, but is born into a noble family;
as a teacher of all sciences and worthy of veneration, he shall attain liberation in the end.
Those who give coral, pearls, gems, diamonds, gold, silver,
and other minerals such as refined gold, shall be freed from sorrow, become fortunate, possess noble lineages, have their faculties complete, and have all their desires fulfilled.
Those whose minds are pure, who offer praise in various forms— whether in prose or verse—
they hear the sounds produced by many musical instruments and the songs of celestial nymphs.
As far as the ground is traversed below, down to the golden wheel,
it is proclaimed to be thousands of yojanas in height from the masses [of earth].
As many as there are grains of sand therein,
so many times shall he become a king, a lord of heroes, a universal monarch upon the earth.
Those who, as soon as they are born, attain lordship, and whose birth is always in the family of a merchant chief,
and who travel about on elephants, horses, and carriages— they do so by having performed prostrations here before the excellent caityas.
Indeed, to whoever offers an oblation with the king of mantras beginning with the syllable *a*,
the gods together with their hosts, being well-satisfied, will grant the desire for the fruits of virtuous deeds.
Those whose bodies are freed from disease, grief, and the like, upon whom they bestow the plaster of nectar,
become lords of wealth, possessors of exceedingly long lives, and the most fortunate among men and gods.
Those fortunate ones who, out of devotion, constantly perform great acts of plastering with clay and cow dung, or prepare pure water-mandalas dedicated to the Buddha, obtain royal power. (Avk 104)
Those people who here diligently cleanse the courtyard of a stūpa, the excellent reliquary, or a monastery,
and who remove the withered flower offerings from these places, become golden-hued and beautiful to behold.
Those who perform circumambulation of that [stupa] become possessors of the recollection of their past lives;
they are golden-hued, blessed with many sons and grandsons, and honored by the assemblies of gods and lords of men.
Even one who performs circumambulation of the Jina’s abode out of mere laziness [attains these fruits].
At every step, one shall obtain the fruit of giving a karṣa of gold.
There is the worship of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and virtuous Śūdras;
those of lower castes than them have no right to perform such worship.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of birds;
indeed, the specific [merit] of perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of birds is now proclaimed.
The lowering of the parasol is prescribed for kings; for Vaiśyas, it is at the offering of food;
and for Śūdras, it is said to be upon the falling of banners, flags, or cloths.
Goldsmiths, blacksmiths, workers in bell-metal, farmers, and others—by the hands of these people here, worship is offered to the preeminent Caityas. (Avk 111)
Rice, condiments, and those who engage in buying and selling—
these should respectfully present their own goods for one's livelihood.
A lamp should be offered with these— namely, *śaulinī*, *dhvananavartī*, *māṃsavartī*, and likewise *surī*— according to the standard of the family dharma.
A leather-worker, a hunter, a government official, a washerman, and a liquor-seller—
having stood at a distance from these, one should pay homage to the temple of the Jina.
Thus, by means of thirty-six types of birth, through the activities of one's own family, and by various other means, the abode of the Jina is to be constantly honored and revered. (Avk 115)
Those whose vows do not waver in their worship of the Supreme Victor should,
out of their own devotion, perform circumambulations and pay homage to him.
Thus, the practitioner of dharma should perform this king of vows day and night ever more;
his merit, as it has been described, shall lead to the destruction of the disease of leprosy.
Even the five sins of immediate retribution will undoubtedly perish;
how much more so other sins, even those committed in previous lives?
O King, there exists no one anywhere in all the worlds who would act otherwise toward this meritorious vow of day and night.
One may remove evil even by hearing [the teaching], and one may obtain merit even by seeing it;
likewise, one gains merit through sympathetic joy—so what then need be said of those who observe the vows?
Having divided the merit of those observing vows into seven parts,
the learned one [the king] receives one part, the charioteer and his men receive one part,
and all sentient beings receive one part; the observer of the vow receives what remains.
Having heard these words of his guru, the great lord was questioned by Indra.
Then, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, he prepared himself to undertake a vow.
Having gone to the city of Vārāṇasī in accordance with the words of Vasubandhu,
and having established a monastery, a royal reliquary (caitya), and a temple for the Jina,
that wise man then provided a feast for the Saṅgha and went to heaven along with the people.
Then, monks, they said this to the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, tiger among sages, you ought to speak again.
O Protector, by whom and by whom was this King of Vows performed in the past?"
The Blessed One said:
"In former times, Śakra performed the vow of the day-and-night fast in the heavens;
having upheld the six perfections, he made offerings to the King of Caityas."
Having always performed circumambulation according to the rules with great festivals. // Avk_125 //
And long ago in the netherworld (pātāla), there was a powerful hero who was the lord of the Daityas,
named Nirghoṣadamana, the crusher of gods and asuras.
Having expelled Indra from heaven and established himself upon the earth,
he brought the three worlds under his own control with the assistance of the asuras.
Having traveled across the circle of the earth, he went to the city of Maghavan; there,
in the great place where Indra had questioned him, he performed five circumambulations before the standing image of the deity and stood at the shore of wisdom.
Having gone again to the netherworlds (pātāla), he practiced that supreme vow;
likewise, the nāginīs and the nāga kings practiced it in the netherworlds.
The King of Caityas, adorned with the hoods of nāgas and fashioned by the lords of gods and nāgas, was constantly worshipped with devotion according to the prescribed rites.
And in former times, the seven sages, being experts in ritual procedures, worshipped with various rites the relics of the Jina established within a reservoir of water.
The female nāgas, blinded by the pride of their poison, caused those honoring the temple of the Jina to be tormented with the burning of poisonous embers.
Then, having been thus sworn by them, those female nāgas said:
"Indeed, for seven births you shall be servants of this caitya."
Then, having again attained human birth at the end [of that life] through the power of merit,
she becomes that very leader who obtains a husband skilled in the Dharma.
Then all those Śambukas, whose minds were fixed on the Dharma, being thus deceived,
performed circumambulations of the grain while meditating upon the abode of the Jina.
Then, through the power of their merit, the seven princesses became fortunate young maidens and attained the supreme state.
Among them, one was named Vratī, who was devoted to her husband and skilled in dharma;
by the power of her merit, Dharmadakṣa obtained the vow.
The righteous Great King Dharmadakṣa, practicing his vow according to the prescribed rule,
together with his wife, that lord of the earth, [was reborn] in Sukhāvatī.
Thus, O monks, having understood this to be the supreme among vows,
one should always attend upon the caityas by means of the practice of the merit of the vow.
There is no merit equal to the vow of the shrine (caityavrata) in the three worlds; this is the truth.
Therefore, the shrine should always be venerated and diligently worshipped. (Avk 140)
Thus ends the narrative of the vow for a day and night.
